s: In the fortieth year, beyond the Jordan in Moab, Moses begins to declare the law to all Israel, recalling the LORD's command at Horeb to leave and possess the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He recounts appointing wise, respected men as heads, captains, and judges over the tribes, and charging the judges to judge impartially. At Kadesh Barnea, after twelve men spied out the land and reported it good, Israel refused to go up, murmuring that the LORD hated them and fearing the Amorites and Anakim. The LORD swore that the evil generation would not see the land except Caleb, barred Moses too, and named Joshua and the little ones as those who would enter. Israel then presumed to attack against the LORD's warning, was routed by the Amorites as far as Hormah, wept without being heard, and stayed many days in Kadesh.

Moses speaks to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the fortieth year, beginning to declare the law and recounting events from Horeb to Kadesh. He says he could not bear the people alone, appointed heads and judges, urged Israel not to fear, and relays that the LORD was angry with him and barred him from entering the land.

Israel is addressed by Moses and reminded that the LORD multiplied them like the stars and commanded them to possess the land. At Kadesh they refused to go up, murmured against the LORD, then presumptuously attacked, were beaten by the Amorites, and wept unheard before staying many days in Kadesh.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 1
s: The LORD commands Israel at Horeb to leave and take the land he swore to their fathers, and goes before them in fire by night and cloud by day. Angered by their unbelief, he swears that the evil generation will not see the land except Caleb, and he refuses to listen to their weeping after their defeat.

Horeb is where the LORD spoke to Israel, telling them they had lived long enough at the mountain and must journey to possess the land. It is also the starting point of an eleven days' journey to Kadesh Barnea by way of Mount Seir.
Kadesh Barnea is reached after travel through the great and terrible wilderness from Horeb. It is the place where Israel refuses to go up, and where they stay many days after their defeat.

The Amorites are named as the people whose hill country Israel is to enter, and Moses recalls that Sihon, king of the Amorites in Heshbon, was struck. When Israel presumptuously went up, the Amorites came out, chased them like bees, and beat them down in Seir as far as Hormah.

l: hill country of the Amorites, Deuteronomy, Chapter 1
s: The hill country of the Amorites is the destination the LORD commands Israel to take, and Israel arrives at it by way of the wilderness. Israel refuses to go up, and later goes up against the LORD's warning and is defeated there.

The land is the one the LORD swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their offspring, and he has set it before Israel. Because of their unbelief, none of the evil generation will see it except Caleb, while Joshua and the little ones are to enter and possess it.

Moses takes twelve men, one from each tribe, at Israel's request to search the land. They go up to the valley of Eshcol, bring back some of its fruit, and report that it is a good land the LORD gives.

Caleb the son of Jephunneh is excepted from the LORD's oath against the evil generation. He will see the land and be given the ground he has trodden on, for him and his children, because he wholly followed the LORD.
Joshua the son of Nun is described as one who stands before Moses and who will go into the land. Moses is told to encourage him, for he will cause Israel to inherit it.

l: Israel's rebellion at Kadesh, Deuteronomy, Chapter 1
s: Israel refuses the command to go up, murmuring that the LORD hated them and fearing the people, fortified cities, and Anakim reported by their brothers. Moses reminds them of the LORD's past care, but they do not believe, and the LORD swears judgment on that generation. They then presume to attack against his warning and are routed.

Speaking in the first person, the narrator recounts how Israel, after circling Mount Seir for many days, was told by the LORD to turn north and pass peacefully through the lands of Esau's descendants, Moab, and Ammon, because the LORD had given those lands to them. The text notes that earlier peoples such as the Emim, Horites, Zamzummim, and Avvim were displaced from these lands. After thirty-eight years from Kadesh Barnea, the generation of men of war had died out, and the LORD commanded Israel to cross the Arnon and begin possessing the land of Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon. Sihon refused passage after Israel offered words of peace, because the LORD hardened his spirit; he fought Israel at Jahaz and was defeated, and Israel destroyed his cities and took the livestock and plunder. Israel did not approach the land of Ammon, as the LORD had forbidden.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 2
s: The LORD directs Israel to turn north from Mount Seir and forbids contending with Esau's descendants, Moab, and Ammon, since he has given each their land. He ensures the old generation of men of war is consumed, then commands Israel to take Sihon's land, hardening Sihon's spirit and delivering him and his people to Israel.

Israel circles Mount Seir many days, then obeys the LORD by passing peacefully by Esau's descendants, Moab, and Ammon and buying food and water. After the generation of men of war dies out, Israel offers Sihon peace, is refused, defeats him at Jahaz, destroys his cities, takes livestock and plunder, and stays away from Ammon's land as forbidden.

l: Esau's descendants (children of Esau), Deuteronomy, Chapter 2
s: Esau's descendants dwell in Seir, which the LORD gave them as a possession, and they are told to be wary because they will fear Israel. Israel is not to contend with them or take their land, and passes by, buying food and water; they had earlier destroyed the Horites and settled in their place.

Israel encircles Mount Seir for many days until the LORD tells them to turn northward. The LORD had given it to Esau as a possession, so Israel may not take any of its land, and the Horites who once lived there were destroyed by Esau's descendants.

Moab's land, Ar, was given by the LORD to the children of Lot, so Israel is told not to bother Moab or fight them, and passes by the way of the wilderness of Moab. Moabites call the earlier tall inhabitants Emim, and they later sold Israel passage as Esau's descendants did.

The land of the children of Ammon was given by the LORD to the children of Lot, so Israel is forbidden to bother them or take their land. It was once a land of Rephaim, whom the Ammonites call Zamzummim, destroyed by the LORD before them; Israel does not come near Ammon's land, including the Jabbok banks.

Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, is given by the LORD into Israel's hand. He refuses Israel passage despite words of peace because the LORD hardened his spirit, comes out with all his people to fight, and is struck down with his sons and people, losing all his cities.
Sihon and all his people came out against Israel to battle at Jahaz. The LORD delivered him up, and Israel struck down Sihon, his sons, and all his people, after which Israel took all his cities.

In Deuteronomy 3, the speaker (who is addressed by the LORD as "me" and later pleads to enter the land, i.e. Moses) recounts how Israel defeated Og, king of Bashan, at Edrei after the LORD told them not to fear. They took all sixty fortified cities of Argob, utterly destroyed the inhabitants, and kept the livestock and plunder. The conquered land east of the Jordan, from the Arnon to Mount Hermon, was distributed: the Reubenites and Gadites received Gilead's southern portion, and the half-tribe of Manasseh received the rest of Gilead and Bashan, with Jair and Machir named in the allotment. The men of valor of these tribes were commanded to cross the Jordan armed ahead of their brothers while their families stayed behind, and Joshua was told not to fear because the LORD fights for Israel. The speaker begged to cross the Jordan and see the good land, but the LORD refused, allowing him only to view it from Pisgah and commanding him to commission Joshua, while they stayed in the valley near Beth Peor.

Og, king of Bashan, came out with all his people to battle Israel at Edrei. The LORD told Israel not to fear him and delivered him and his people into their hand, and they struck them until none remained. He was the last of the remnant of the Rephaim, and his iron bedstead was nine cubits long and four wide.

Bashan was the kingdom of Og, containing sixty fortified cities in the region of Argob plus many unwalled villages. Israel took it, and it was given to the half-tribe of Manasseh; Jair named the Argob region Havvoth Jair after himself. It is also called the land of Rephaim.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 3
s: The LORD told Moses not to fear Og and delivered Og and his people into Israel's hand as he had done with Sihon. He fights for Israel, as Joshua is told, but was angry with Moses because of the people and refused his request to cross the Jordan, permitting him only to view the land from Pisgah.

Moses, as the speaker, recounts the defeat of Og, the taking of the land east of the Jordan, and his gifts of land to Reubenites, Gadites, Manasseh, and Machir. He commanded the eastern tribes and Joshua, and begged the LORD to let him cross the Jordan, but was refused and told to view the land from Pisgah and commission Joshua.

The Israelites went up the way to Bashan, defeated Og and his people, took all his cities, and utterly destroyed the inhabitants while taking the livestock and plunder. They took the land from the two Amorite kings between the Arnon and Mount Hermon, and remained in the valley near Beth Peor.

Gilead was taken with the other cities of the plain and Bashan. Half the hill country of Gilead went to the Reubenites and Gadites, the rest to the half-tribe of Manasseh, and Gilead was also given to Machir.

The Reubenites received land from Aroer by the Arnon valley and half the hill country of Gilead, extending to the Jabbok, along with the Arabah and Jordan border. Their men of valor were commanded to cross the Jordan armed before their brothers, while their families and livestock stayed in the cities.

The Gadites, together with the Reubenites, received land from Aroer and half the hill country of Gilead to the Jabbok, plus the Arabah and the Jordan and its border. Their men of valor were to cross over armed ahead of their brothers until the other tribes received rest.

The half-tribe of Manasseh was given the rest of Gilead and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, including all the region of Argob. Jair the son of Manasseh took the Argob region and named it Havvoth Jair after himself.

Moses commanded Joshua, reminding him that his eyes had seen what the LORD did to the two kings and that the LORD would do the same to all kingdoms ahead, so he should not fear. Joshua is to be commissioned, encouraged, and strengthened, since he will lead the people across the Jordan and cause them to inherit the land.

Sixty cities in the region of Argob, fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, plus many unwalled villages, made up Og's kingdom. Israel took every one and utterly destroyed them, including women and little ones, keeping the livestock and plunder.

After Og attacked at Edrei, the LORD delivered him into Israel's hand as with Sihon, and Israel struck down his people until none remained. They took all sixty cities, destroyed the inhabitants, and kept livestock and plunder, taking the land from the Arnon to Mount Hermon.

l: Moses' request to enter the land, Deuteronomy, Chapter 3
s: Moses begged the LORD, praising his greatness and incomparable works, to let him cross the Jordan and see the good land, the fine mountain, and Lebanon. The LORD, angry because of the people, refused and told him to speak no more of it, but to go up to Pisgah and view the land in every direction and to commission Joshua.

In Deuteronomy 4, Moses urges Israel to obey the statutes and ordinances he teaches so that they may live and possess the land the LORD gives them, and he warns them neither to add to nor take from the commandments. He recalls the LORD's judgment on those who followed Baal Peor and the day at Horeb when the LORD spoke from the fire without any visible form, which is the basis for forbidding carved images and the worship of the sun, moon, and stars. Moses tells them he will die east of the Jordan, warns that idolatry will bring scattering among the nations, yet promises that the merciful LORD will be found when they seek him with all their heart. He points to the LORD's unique acts in bringing Israel out of Egypt as proof that the LORD alone is God, and calls them to keep his commandments. Finally, Moses sets apart three cities beyond the Jordan for unintentional killers, and the chapter introduces the law he set before Israel in the valley opposite Beth Peor, in the land taken from Sihon and Og.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 4
s: The LORD destroyed those who followed Baal Peor, spoke to Israel from the fire at Horeb, and brought them out of Egypt with signs, wonders, and a mighty hand. He is described as a devouring fire and a jealous God, yet also merciful, and he will not forget the covenant with their fathers. He is declared to be the only God in heaven above and on the earth beneath.

Moses teaches Israel the statutes and ordinances as the LORD commanded him, urging obedience and warning against adding to or taking away from them. He reveals that the LORD was angry with him for the people's sakes and swore he would not cross the Jordan, so he must die in the land east of it. He also sets apart three cities beyond the Jordan and sets the law before the Israelites.

Israel is addressed as a people who saw the LORD's acts at Baal Peor and heard his voice from the fire at Horeb, and those who stayed faithful are alive. They are called to obey, teach their children, and avoid idolatry, with a warning that disobedience will bring scattering and few survivors among the nations. The text also says they will seek the LORD there, find him, and return, because he chose them and brought them out of Egypt to be his inheritance.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 4
s: The statutes and ordinances are taught by Moses as commanded by the LORD, and Israel is told not to add to or take from them. Keeping them is called Israel's wisdom and understanding in the sight of the peoples, who will see that no other great nation has such righteous law. Obedience is tied to living well and prolonging days in the land.

Horeb is where Israel stood before the LORD when the mountain burned with fire amid darkness, cloud, and thick darkness. The LORD spoke from the fire, and the people heard a voice but saw no form. There he declared his covenant, the ten commandments, and wrote them on two stone tablets.

l: carved images and idolatry, Deuteronomy, Chapter 4
s: Israel is forbidden to make a carved image in the form of any figure, whether human, animal, bird, creeping thing, or fish, since they saw no form at Horeb. They are also warned not to be drawn into worshiping the sun, moon, and stars. Idolatry is said to bring utter destruction and scattering, with exile among gods of wood and stone that cannot see, hear, eat, or smell.

The land across the Jordan is the good land the LORD gives Israel as an inheritance, to be possessed by driving out nations greater and mightier than they. Moses says he will not enter it but Israel will. Remaining long in it depends on faithfulness, and idolatry would mean being removed from it.

l: three cities of refuge, Deuteronomy, Chapter 4
s: Moses sets apart three cities beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise so that a man who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without prior hatred, can flee there and live. They are Bezer in the wilderness for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.

Moses summons all Israel to hear the statutes and ordinances, reminding them that the LORD made his covenant at Horeb with those alive today, speaking face to face out of the fire while Moses stood between them because they were afraid. Moses recites the commandments the LORD spoke: no other gods, no carved images, no misuse of his name, keeping the Sabbath in remembrance of Egypt, honoring parents, and prohibitions against murder, adultery, stealing, false testimony, and coveting. The LORD wrote the words on two stone tablets and gave them to Moses. The people, terrified by the fire and voice, ask Moses to go near and hear the rest and tell them, promising to hear and do it. The LORD approves their words, longs for a heart in them to fear him, sends them back to their tents, and tells Moses to stay and receive the commandments, statutes, and ordinances to teach them for life in the land. Moses closes by urging Israel to walk in all the LORD's way without turning aside.

Moses calls all Israel to hear and observe the statutes and ordinances, and recounts how he stood between the LORD and the people at Horeb because they feared the fire. He received the two stone tablets, relayed the people's request to hear the LORD through him, and was told to stay with the LORD to receive all the commandments, statutes, and ordinances to teach the people.

Israel is addressed as the generation alive today with whom the covenant was made. At Horeb they feared the fire and voice, asked Moses to go near and speak for the LORD, and promised to hear and do what he told them. The LORD approved their words, sent them back to their tents, and they are urged to walk in his way without turning right or left.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 5
s: The LORD spoke face to face out of the fire, cloud, and thick darkness with a great voice, declared the commandments, wrote them on two stone tablets, and gave them to Moses. He describes himself as a jealous God who visits iniquity on the generations that hate him and shows loving kindness to thousands who love him. He approved the people's response, wished they would fear him always, and told Moses to stay to receive further commandments.

The covenant was made by the LORD at Horeb, and Moses stresses that it was made not with the fathers but with the very people alive and present that day. The commandments spoken from the fire form its content in this unit.

The words are recited here: no other gods, no carved image, no bowing to or serving images, no misuse of the LORD's name, Sabbath observance, honoring father and mother, and not murdering, committing adultery, stealing, giving false testimony, or coveting. The LORD spoke them to the whole assembly with a great voice, added no more, and wrote them on two stone tablets given to Moses.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 5
s: Moses opens by calling Israel to hear the statutes and ordinances so they may learn and observe them. The LORD tells Moses to stay beside him so he can receive all the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that Moses is to teach the people for keeping in the land.

The Sabbath is to be kept holy as the LORD commanded. After six days of labor, the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD on which no work is done by the people, their household, servants, animals, or the stranger within their gates, so servants may rest too. It is tied to remembering that Israel was a servant in Egypt and was brought out by a mighty hand and outstretched arm.

The land is described as one the LORD gives them to possess, where they are to do the commandments. Honoring parents is linked to long days in it, and walking in the LORD's way is linked to living well and prolonging their days there.

In Chapter 6, Moses-style address to Israel presents the LORD's commandments, statutes, and ordinances to be kept in the land they are about to possess, so that they may fear the LORD and prosper. Israel is told to hear that the LORD is one and to love him with all their heart, soul, and might, keeping his words on their hearts, teaching them to their children, and binding and writing them on hands, foreheads, door posts, and gates. They are warned that when the LORD brings them into a land of cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards, and olive trees they did not build or plant, they must not forget him who brought them out of Egypt, must not follow other gods, and must not tempt him as at Massah. When their son asks the meaning of the laws, they are to tell him of slavery under Pharaoh in Egypt and the LORD's mighty deliverance, and that keeping all the commandments will be righteousness for them.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 6
s: The LORD your God is declared to be one and is to be loved with all the heart, soul, and might, feared, served, and sworn by. He is a jealous God whose anger would destroy those who follow other gods. He brought Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders and swore the land to their fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Israel is commanded to hear, love the LORD, keep his words on their hearts, teach them to their children, and not forget him once they are prosperous in the land. They are forbidden to follow other gods or tempt the LORD as at Massah. They are told that observing all the commandments will be righteousness to them.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 6
s: The commandments, statutes, and ordinances are given so Israel may do them in the land, fear the LORD, and have long and good lives. They are to be taught diligently, bound on hand and forehead, and written on door posts and gates. Keeping them is said to be for Israel's good always and counts as righteousness.

The land was sworn by the LORD to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and is described as flowing with milk and honey. It holds great and good cities, full houses, dug cisterns, vineyards, and olive trees that Israel did not build or plant. Israel is to possess it and thrust out their enemies, but must not forget the LORD when they are full there.

Egypt is the land where Israel was in slavery, called the house of bondage, under Pharaoh. The LORD showed great and awesome signs and wonders on Egypt, Pharaoh, and all his house before Israel's eyes.

The son is to be taught the LORD's words diligently by his parent, together with later generations. When he asks what the testimonies, statutes, and ordinances mean, he is to be told of Israel's slavery in Egypt, the LORD's deliverance, and the purpose of the laws for their good.

l: signs and wonders in Egypt, Deuteronomy, Chapter 6
s: The exodus is recalled as the LORD bringing Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand, with great signs and wonders against Pharaoh and his house. It was done so that he might bring them into the land sworn to their fathers. Israel is warned not to forget it, and it is the answer to give a son who asks about the laws.

Chapter 7 gives the Israelites instructions for entering the land, where the LORD your God will cast out seven nations greater and mightier than they: the Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite. The Israelites are told to utterly destroy these nations, make no covenant or marriages with them, and break down their altars, pillars, Asherah poles, and engraved images, lest they be led to serve other gods. The text grounds this in Israel's status as a holy people chosen not for its size but because the LORD loves them and keeps the oath sworn to their fathers. Obedience to the commandments, statutes, and ordinances is promised to bring blessings of fertility, abundant produce and livestock, and freedom from sickness, while those who hate the LORD are repaid. The Israelites are told not to fear the larger nations, to remember what the LORD did to Pharaoh and Egypt, and to expect the nations to be driven out little by little, and they must not covet the silver and gold on the idols lest they become a devoted thing.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 7
s: The LORD your God brings the Israelites into the land, casts out the seven nations, delivers them and their kings into Israel's hand, and sends the hornet and a great confusion among them. He is described as the faithful God who keeps covenant and loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love him, and who repays those who hate him to their face. He chose Israel out of love and the oath to the fathers, redeemed them from Pharaoh, and promises blessing for obedience.

The Israelites are addressed as a holy people chosen by the LORD as his own possession, not because they were many but because they were the fewest. They are commanded to destroy the nations, avoid covenants and intermarriage, destroy idolatrous objects, not covet the silver and gold on them, keep the commandments, and not fear the greater nations. If they obey, they will be blessed above all peoples.

l: seven nations of Canaan, Deuteronomy, Chapter 7
s: The Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite are named as seven nations greater and mightier than Israel. The LORD will cast them out little by little, confuse them, deliver their kings to Israel, and make their name perish from under the sky. Israel is forbidden to make covenants or marriages with them or show them mercy.

The land is the place the Israelites are going to possess, which the LORD swore to their fathers to give them. The LORD will bless the fruit of its ground, including grain, new wine, and oil. The nations are to be driven out gradually so that the animals of the field do not increase against Israel.

Other gods are what the nations' influence could lead Israel's sons to serve if intermarriage occurs, which would kindle the LORD's anger. Israel is told not to serve their gods, because doing so would be a snare. The engraved images of these gods are to be burned, and they are called an abomination.

l: idolatrous objects (altars, pillars, Asherah poles, engraved images), Deuteronomy, Chapter 7
s: The Israelites are commanded to break down the nations' altars, dash their pillars in pieces, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their engraved images with fire. They must not covet or take the silver and gold on the images, nor bring an abomination into their house. Doing so would make them a devoted thing like it, so they must utterly detest and abhor it.

l: covenant (oath to the fathers), Deuteronomy, Chapter 7
s: The LORD's desire to keep the oath he swore to Israel's fathers is given as a reason for bringing Israel out of Egypt. The LORD keeps covenant and loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commandments. If Israel listens to and keeps the ordinances, he will keep the covenant and loving kindness with them. Israel itself is forbidden to make a covenant with the nations of the land.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 7
s: The Israelites are told to keep and do the commandments, statutes, and ordinances commanded that day. The LORD's keeping of the covenant and loving kindness is tied to Israel's listening to and obeying them. Keeping them is presented as the condition for the blessings.

l: utter destruction of the nations, Deuteronomy, Chapter 7
s: When the LORD delivers the nations up and Israel strikes them, Israel is commanded to utterly destroy them, showing no mercy and no pity. The text says the nations will be consumed little by little rather than at once, and that no one will be able to stand before Israel until they are destroyed. The reason given is to prevent covenants, marriages, and idolatry that would turn Israel from the LORD.

For obeying the ordinances, the LORD promises to love, bless, and multiply Israel, and to bless their offspring, ground, grain, new wine, oil, livestock, and flocks. Israel will be blessed above all peoples, with no barrenness among people or livestock. The LORD will remove all sickness and the evil diseases of Egypt from them and lay those on all who hate them.

In Chapter 8, the speaker exhorts the Israelites to keep all the commandments so that they may live, multiply, and possess the land the LORD swore to their fathers. He reminds them that the LORD led them forty years in the wilderness to humble and test them, feeding them with manna and keeping their clothing and feet from wearing out, as a father disciplines a son. He describes the good land they are entering, rich in water, grain, fruit, olive trees, honey, iron, and copper. He warns that prosperity could lead them to forget the LORD and claim their wealth as the work of their own power. He declares that the LORD gives the power to get wealth, and that if they forget him and serve other gods, they will perish like the nations the LORD destroys before them.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 8
s: The LORD your God led the Israelites forty years in the wilderness to humble and test them, fed them with manna, provided water from the flint rock, and disciplined them as a man disciplines his son. He is bringing them into a good land, and it is he who gives them power to get wealth in order to establish his covenant sworn to their fathers. He testifies that those who forget him and follow other gods will perish as the nations he destroys.

The Israelites are commanded to keep all the commandments, remember the wilderness years, and bless the LORD when they eat and are full in the land. They are warned not to forget him or to credit their own power for their wealth. If they forget him and worship other gods, they will surely perish like the nations destroyed before them.

The wilderness is where the LORD led the Israelites for forty years to humble and test them and to learn what was in their hearts. It is described as great and terrible, with venomous snakes, scorpions, and thirsty ground. There the LORD fed them with manna, brought water out of flint rock, and kept their clothing from growing old and their feet from swelling.

The good land is the one the LORD swore to their fathers and is bringing the Israelites into. It has brooks, springs, and underground water, and produces wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, pomegranates, olive trees, and honey. It lacks nothing, with stones of iron and hills from which copper can be dug, and the Israelites are to bless the LORD for it.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 8
s: The commandments are what the Israelites are told to observe so that they may live, multiply, and possess the land. Keeping them means walking in the LORD's ways and fearing him, and the wilderness testing was to see whether they would keep them. Forgetting the LORD means not keeping his commandments, ordinances, and statutes, which leads to perishing.

Moses addresses Israel as they are about to cross the Jordan to dispossess great, fortified nations including the tall sons of Anak. He tells them the LORD will go before them as a devouring fire, but that they are receiving the land because of the nations' wickedness and the LORD's oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, not because of their own righteousness, for they are stiff-necked. Moses recounts Israel's rebellion at Horeb: while he was on the mountain forty days and nights receiving the stone tablets, the people made a molten calf, the LORD threatened to destroy them, and Moses broke the tablets, burned and ground the calf, and threw its dust into the brook. He recalls falling down before the LORD another forty days and nights, praying for Israel and Aaron, and lists further provocations at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh Barnea. His prayer asks the LORD to remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and not destroy the people who are his inheritance.
